payload.content: The sky is blue because of Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight is a mix of wavelengths, and when it passes through the atmosphere it is scattered by nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. The amount of scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength, so short blue wavelengths are scattered roughly five to six times more strongly than red. That scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every direction of the sky. The sky looks blue rather than violet because sunlight contains less violet, some is absorbed in the upper atmosphere, and human eyes are more sensitive to blue.

Short answer: air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths much more than long (red) wavelengths — Rayleigh scattering scales as 1/λ⁴. So when you look away from the Sun you mostly see scattered blue light. At sunset the light path is long, blue is scattered out, and the remaining direct light looks red/orange.
